Proclaim
pro-KLAME
v.t. (to cry aloud publicly with authority; rendering Hebrew qara, Greek kerusso)
From Latin proclamare, to cry out — pro, forth, and clamare, to shout. The Latin keeps the herald's posture: a proclamation is not an argument offered but a decree announced by a man who did not write it.

Biblical Definition

To proclaim is to publish a decree on someone else's authority, and the first and greatest instance has God as the herald of His own name: “I will make all my goodness pass before thee, and I will proclaim the name of the LORD before thee; and will be gracious to whom I will be gracious” (Exodus 33:19). Everything the herald's office means is there — the content is God's character, the timing is God's choosing, and the sovereignty of the mercy is stated in the same sentence, which is why Paul quotes precisely this verse in Romans 9:15 to establish unconditional election. The word then governs the calendar: Israel's feasts are not customs that arose but convocations she is commanded to announce, “the feasts of the LORD, which ye shall proclaim to be holy convocations” (Leviticus 23:2). It governs the economy: in the jubilee year Israel must “proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof” (Leviticus 25:10), the verse cast on the Liberty Bell. And it governs the Messiah's ministry, where the jubilee language returns as gospel: the Anointed is sent “to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound” (Isaiah 61:1), the text the Lord read at Nazareth and closed the book upon. Preaching in the New Testament is kerusso, this same herald's work: not persuasion, discussion, or exploration, but the public announcement of a finished decree.

Webster 1828 Definition

To announce publicly on another's authority. God proclaims His own name to Moses; Israel proclaims the feasts and the jubilee liberty; and the Messiah is sent to proclaim liberty to captives — the pattern behind New Testament preaching.

PROCLAIM, v.t. [L. proclamo; pro and clamo, to cry out.] To promulgate; to announce; to publish; as, to proclaim a fast.

2. To denounce; to give official notice of.

3. To declare with honor; as, to proclaim the name of the Lord. Ex. 33.

4. To outlaw by public denunciation.

PROCLAMATION, n. The act of announcing or publishing by authority; official notice given to the public.

Key Scripture

Exodus 33:19 — "And he said, I will make all my goodness pass before thee, and I will proclaim the name of the LORD before thee; and will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will shew mercy on whom I will shew mercy."

Leviticus 23:2 — "Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, Concerning the feasts of the LORD, which ye shall proclaim to be holy convocations, even these are my feasts."

Leviticus 25:10 — "And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family."

Isaiah 61:1 — "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;"

Modern Corruption

Preaching has been redefined from proclamation into conversation — the herald replaced by the facilitator, the decree replaced by the shared exploration — and the shift is defended as humility when it is in fact a change of office.

expand to see more

A herald has no authority over his message and no permission to soften it; that is the whole point of the office, and it is why Scripture chose the word. When preaching is recast as dialogue, story-sharing, or a journey undertaken alongside the hearers, the man in the pulpit has silently exchanged the herald's commission for the moderator's. The change is usually presented as a virtue — who am I to declare? — but Scripture treats the reluctance as disobedience, not modesty. Paul's charge is to “preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” and to do it as one who knows that men will not endure sound doctrine (2 Timothy 4:2-3). A herald who takes a vote on the decree has not humbled himself; he has deserted his post.

The jubilee texts are corrupted in a second direction, by being read as a political programme detached from their covenantal frame. Leviticus 25 proclaims liberty because the land belongs to the LORD and Israel are His tenants, and the release is tied to atonement — the jubilee is announced on the day of atonement itself (Leviticus 25:9). Isaiah 61:1 takes that machinery and applies it to the release of sinners, which is exactly how the Lord Jesus applied it in the synagogue at Nazareth. To lift the language of proclaimed liberty out of that setting and make it a slogan for economic redistribution keeps the vocabulary and discards the atonement that funds it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qara (to call, cry, proclaim) and shama in the causative (to cause to be heard); Greek kerusso (to herald) and katangello (to announce down to).

expand to see more

Hebrew qara (H7121) — to call out, cry, proclaim; the verb in Exodus 33:19, Leviticus 23:2, Leviticus 25:10, and Isaiah 61:1.

Hebrew deror (H1865) — liberty, a flowing free; the noun proclaimed in Leviticus 25:10 and Isaiah 61:1.

Greek kerusso (G2784) — to herald, to publish a decree as a public crier; the standard New Testament word for preaching.

Greek keryx (G2783) — the herald himself; Paul calls himself one in 1 Timothy 2:7 and 2 Timothy 1:11.

Greek katangello (G2605) — to announce, declare thoroughly; used of proclaiming the Lord's death in 1 Corinthians 11:26.

Usage

"“I will proclaim the name of the LORD before thee” — God is the first herald of His own character, and He sets the terms of the mercy in the same breath."

"“Proclaim liberty throughout all the land” — the jubilee release, announced on the day of atonement."

"“To proclaim liberty to the captives” — the jubilee taken up as the gospel and read by Christ at Nazareth."
